CLEAR: Capability-Aware Latent Ordering for Adaptive Interaction with Movable Objects

Anonymous Authors / Under Review

TL;DR

CLEAR jointly selects objects, determines their interaction order, and generates motion references conditioned on robot morphology and scene geometry.

Same scene, different bodies

A humanoid pushes a box, a quadruped crosses steps, and a wheeled robot follows a slope to reach the same goal. Robot morphology determines terrain traversability and feasible object interactions. Planning must account for these constraints and for how each interaction affects subsequent actions.

Method

Pipeline(a) Grounding(b) Selection and ordering(c) Generation(d) Execution and replanning

From the body to a plan.

CLEAR plans how a robot can reach its goal by moving objects in the scene. It decides which objects to move, in what order, and how to move them, taking the robot’s capabilities and the effects of earlier interactions into account.

Affordance-Guided Encoding builds a planning context that reflects the robot’s interaction capabilities and object reachability. Shared feature encoding and average pooling turn the link, joint, and actuator properties of embodiment into an embedding .

Conditioned on this embedding and local scene observations, the network predicts an affordance probability for each candidate object interaction or terrain transition. The binary label indicates interaction availability or transition feasibility.

When terrain limits movement, path search uses predicted transition probabilities to evaluate scene connectivity and determine which objects are reachable. Object features augmented with these interaction probabilities and reachability information are combined with and scene observations to form , the shared input to OrderNet and CausalFlowNet.

From , OrderNet predicts a selection probability and Gaussian score parameters for each object. Bernoulli sampling selects the object set ; Gaussian sampling produces latent scores . Sorting selected scores from lowest to highest determines the interaction order.

Sampling produces alternative object sets and sequences for the same scene and embodiment. Selection considers the complete sequence, including objects that become reachable after earlier interactions. Each candidate uses an object at most once; replanning may select that object again.

Binary cross-entropy trains selection. A weighted Bradley–Terry loss encourages lower scores for preceding objects, with more weight on nearby pairs in the training order. Gaussian reparameterization supports gradient-based score learning, and KL regularization keeps the score distributions close to a standard normal distribution.

CausalFlowNet generates continuous object parameters with the selected set, interaction order, and planning context held fixed. Rank is an object’s position in . The matrix stores coordinates per object; is generation time, not execution time.

Rank-causal attention gives each selected object access to its own token, preceding ranks, and . Generated information cannot enter context tokens, so later predictions cannot influence earlier ones indirectly through the shared context.

During training, active coordinates of selected objects exclude padding and fixed coordinates. Independent Gaussian noise initializes these coordinates in , and is sampled for conditional flow matching:

The loss is mean squared error over active coordinates, averaged over training examples, noise, and flow time; it is zero when no active coordinates exist. The combined objective adds ordering, flow, affordance, and optional availability losses:

The availability term uses training labels to penalize unavailable objects, with normalized first-interaction weights proportional to ; when unused.

At inference, integrating from Gaussian noise at to produces . Selected rows are decoded in order into object targets or trajectories . Different noise samples yield alternative motions under the same selection and order; the resulting candidates proceed to feasibility checking.

Candidate validation checks robot reachability, collision avoidance, and interaction constraints in interaction order . Each check uses the scene resulting from preceding object motions. This validation step is omitted in the Grid and Ordered Manipulation evaluations.

Among feasible candidates that satisfy the navigation or arrangement goal , the planner selects the one with the fewest object interactions. A valid candidate requiring no interaction has and bypasses continuous generation.

For legged robots, an MPC-based controller evaluates candidate command sequences through rollouts of a learned locomotion policy. Quality-diversity optimization retains high-performing and behaviorally diverse sequences, combined with Cartesian tracking and joint-command smoothing.

The controller executes an initial segment of the best evaluated command sequence and updates its optimization using new state estimates. After each object interaction, updated scene observations guide replanning of the remaining interactions.

Robot embodiment is described by link, joint, and actuator properties. Shared feature encoding and average pooling construct the embedding , which conditions predictions of interaction availability and terrain-transition feasibility.

Each movable object has a current configuration and physical attributes , including geometry and mass. Object motions change the scene and can make subsequent interactions reachable.

The scene contains observed environment geometry, the current robot state, movable objects, and task goal . The goal specifies a navigation destination or desired object arrangement. Terrain connectivity determines which objects the robot can reach.

Ground the scene in the robot’s body.

Structure, object states, and scene geometry form a planning context that represents the robot’s capabilities and accessible interactions.

(a) Embodiment-Aware Scene Grounding

Affordance-Guided Encoding combines morphology, object and scene features into the planning context . Predicted traversal and interaction feasibility augment the object features. Reachability accounts for the terrain transitions needed to approach an object.

Accessibility

Accessibility describes whether the robot can reach a feasible contact configuration around an object.

Capability

Capability describes the robot motions and contact actions available for executing an interaction.

(b) Latent Interaction Ordering

From , OrderNet predicts a selection probability and priority mean and standard deviation for each object . A sampled indicator determines participation. Sorting sampled scores from low to high gives the order .

Sampling admits alternative object sets and orders for the same query. Selection considers the complete sequence, including objects that become reachable after earlier interactions.

In this scene. blocks the first passage. Moving it creates access to . The example order is , while remains outside the route.

(c) Rank-Causal Generation

With fixed, CausalFlowNet integrates from Gaussian noise in the active coordinates of to . In , row stores coordinates for object . Fixed and padding coordinates remain unchanged. The selected rows are decoded in order into references . Flow time describes generation progress, not execution time.

All selected rows evolve over the same flow interval. Rank causal attention lets each row read its own and preceding ranks. Context tokens cannot read generated rows, preventing later interactions from influencing earlier ones through .

In this scene. relocates to clear the first passage. plans the motion of with access through that passage. Feasibility is checked after generation.

(d) Execution and Replanning

Decoded references are checked in order , accounting for the scene changes caused by earlier interactions. The planner selects a candidate that satisfies the goal with the fewest interactions among those accepted. A valid plan requiring no object interaction bypasses generation. MPC tracks the object references using updated state estimates. When enabled, replanning uses the updated scene to revise the remaining interactions.

CLEAR evaluates candidate commands through policy rollouts, retains high performing and behaviorally diverse candidates, and combines Cartesian tracking with joint command smoothing. The controller executes an initial segment and updates its plan using new observations.

CLEAR jointly learns object selection, interaction order, conditional targets and embodiment conditioned affordances.

Loading recorded losses…

The plotted run uses λflow = 1, λKL = 0.001, λaff = 1 and λavail = 0. The availability term is inactive in this run. Hover a curve to inspect its recorded values.

Component objectives

Choose the objects, then learn their relative order.

Selection BCE trains each participation probability . Ranking trains lower latent scores for objects that should come first. KL regularization keeps the score distributions near a standard normal, with weight 0.001 in this run. The selected objects and their sorted scores define the sequence that conditions generation.

Inspect reference plans →
Generate the object motion under the chosen order.

Flow matching trains a velocity field from Gaussian noise toward reference object configurations or trajectories. Generation keeps the selected set and order fixed; rank-causal attention lets an object use earlier ranks. This loss trains continuous targets, while selection and ranking train the discrete sequence.

Inspect generated object references →
Ground the plan in what the robot can reach and interact with.

Affordance BCE learns binary interaction availability or terrain-transition feasibility from labels. These predictions augment object features and reachability information in the shared planning context used by both OrderNet and CausalFlowNet.

Inspect feasibility samples →
Discourage an unavailable first interaction.

The auxiliary penalty uses availability labels and normalized first-interaction weights proportional to . It links object selection and priority scores to which interaction can start the plan; an object may still become reachable after an earlier interaction.

Inactive in this run: . Its contribution to the full objective is zero. No availability-loss curve was logged.

Scene and protocol

Five scene families isolate direct navigation, a single obstruction, interaction chains, branching alternatives, and irrelevant objects. Six planners are replayed on the same scene within each family. These evaluations execute the generated plan without a separate feasibility filter.

Blue denotes the robot and green denotes the goal. Colored blocks are movable objects. Each tile is an individual recorded episode, not an aggregate success rate. Playback preserves discrete grid transitions.

Scene and protocol

A UR5e arm manipulates a cube, two buttons, a drawer, and a sliding window. Button requirements determine when the drawer and window become available. The evaluation tests unseen combinations of those requirements. All methods share an MPC controller and replan after interactions.

This scene compares CLEAR with classical search, behavior cloning, a shared grounding variant, and separately trained ablations of affordance conditioning and causal attention. Goal completion and precondition violations are reported separately for each displayed episode.

The interactive replays preserve recorded joint configurations and button states. Results shown under individual clips are not aggregate success rates.

Scene and protocol

The evaluation considers G1, Spot, Spot with an arm, and Husky in shared environments with terrain and movable obstacles. Standard scenes vary traversability and interaction requirements. High mass scenes include objects weighing 11.5 kg. Each embodiment uses a fixed controller across planning methods.

The available replays below isolate high mass interactions for G1 and Spot with an arm, followed by a terrain comparison for G1. The full evaluation additionally measures planning accuracy for Husky. These selected scenes illustrate individual behaviors rather than every evaluated trial.

Execution replays use the recorded physical states. When a planner returned no valid plan and no trajectory was recorded, its tile shows the initial scene with a start marker. It does not simulate an unobserved failure.

Validation and replanning depend on the experimental protocol. Grid and Ordered Manipulation omit separate feasibility validation. Maze Navigation comparisons omit high-level replanning.

Scene and protocol

The experiment compares CLEAR with a variant that retains its initial plan. Both share the learned checkpoint, controller, and execution limits. The paper evaluates nominal execution, displaced target objects, and changes in access to later interactions. Low level feedback alone cannot revise the high level interaction sequence.

The paired replays show how the planner responds to external object relocations and updates the remaining interactions.

Each replay retains its own recorded simulation duration. The pair is not time synchronized. Object relocations are external disturbances, not robot interactions.
